definition: Grammatik was the first grammar-checking program for home computers.
details: Aspen Software of Albuquerque, NM, released the earliest version of this diction and style checker for personal computers. It was first released no later than 1981, and was inspired by the Writer's Workbench. Grammatik was first available for the TRS-80, and soon had versions for CP/M and the IBM PC. Reference Software International of San Francisco, California, acquired Grammatik in 1985. Development of Grammatik continued, and it became an actual grammar checker that could detect writing errors beyond simple style checking. Subsequent versions were released for MS-DOS, Windows, Macintosh, and Unix. Grammatik was ultimately acquired by WordPerfect Corporation and is integrated into the WordPerfect word processor.

explainer.lead: Grammatik was an early writing assistant for personal computers, initially checking diction and style before developing into a fuller grammar checker. Its journey from the TRS-80 to integration in WordPerfect helped bring automated writing feedback into everyday word processing.

tiers.eli5: Grammatik was like a helpful reader inside an early home computer, pointing out ways a piece of writing could be improved. At first it looked at word choice and writing style, and later it could also find grammar problems. It eventually became part of WordPerfect, so people could check their writing while using that word processor.
tiers.practitioner: Grammatik should be treated as a historical end-user writing tool whose behavior depends strongly on version and platform. Early releases performed diction and style checking, while later releases detected writing errors beyond simple style issues. Implementations appeared across several desktop and Unix environments, with later access through WordPerfect rather than only as a separate checker.
tiers.paperLevel: Grammatik can be described as a personal-computer writing-analysis tool: input = document text; output = diction and style feedback in early versions, followed in later versions by detection of a broader range of writing errors. It was inspired by Writer's Workbench. The earliest versions were not full grammar checkers, and their checking scope should not be conflated with that of later releases.

explainer.example: An early TRS-80 user could run Grammatik on a document to check its diction and style. A later WordPerfect user could use its developed grammar-checking capability within the word processor.

explainer.intuition: The basic idea was to give computer users an automated second reader for their prose. It began by reviewing diction and style, then expanded to identify grammar and other writing errors.
howItWorks: A writer prepared a document on a supported personal computer.
Early versions of Grammatik checked the writing for diction and style issues.
Continued development added detection of writing errors beyond simple style checking.
Later users could work with the checker on additional operating systems or through its integration into WordPerfect.
explainer.whyItMatters: Released no later than 1981, Grammatik was the first grammar-checking program for home computers. Its development and eventual WordPerfect integration mark an early step toward writing assistance becoming a standard part of personal-computer software.
misconceptions: It was not first written for the IBM PC; the TRS-80 version came first.
The earliest release was a diction and style checker, not yet a full grammar checker.
WordPerfect did not create it; Aspen Software released it, Reference Software International acquired it in 1985, and WordPerfect Corporation acquired it later.
